newsitem.title: CHINA: China T-bills become top market on bank rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: China T-bills become top market on bank rate cuts.

text.p: For the first time ever, China's treasury bills market was the nation's most active last month, with prices surging after a deep cut in bank interest rates by the central bank, analysts said on Monday.
In Shanghai, trading of T-bills, or short-term government bonds, far outpaced share turnover as retail and institution investors piled into the market.
The analysts said the T-bill market was unlikely to maintain its hectic pace and with the rate cut already digested, trading was set to calm down over coming months.
But they said a series of reforms this year would ensure the trading of T-bills would remain one of China's most active financial markets.

Figures issued on Monday by the Shanghai stock exchange, home to China's biggest T-bill trading floor, show trading in August hit a monthly record of 288.7 billion yuan ($34.78 billion), with T-bill spots accounting for 131.6 billion yuan and repurchases 157.1 billion yuan.
This compares with 63.7 billion yuan in trading of stocks, which until August was China's most active financial market.
Traders said the main factor for the record T-bill trading was the rumour and reality of a rate cut by the central bank.

On August 23, the People's Bank of China cut interest rates for bank deposits and loans by an average 1.5 and 1.2 percentage points respectively. Rumours of the cut began to circulate in the market from the end of July.
"Price and turnover surges on the T-bill market in August were mainly due to the bank interest rate cut," said Lu Weimin, a bond trader with China Guotai Securities.
"With T-bill coupons fixed, the cut has made their returns much higher than returns on bank deposits," he added.

On August 21, when media reports said the cut would be announced in one or two days, the 10-year bond that matures in June 2006 -- and regarded as a barometer of the market -- soared 5.66 yuan, or 4.87 percent, in Shanghai. It was the highest single-day rise for a bond since China revived the market in 1992.
On August 26, the newest three-year bond that matures in August 1999 opened in Shanghai at 106.80 yuan, up 6.8 percent from an issue price of 100 yuan, the strongest debut by a bond since 1992.

The three-year bond bears an annual coupon of 10.96 percent, the lowest level for a three-year bill in China for four years, but still higher than the annual 8.28 percent paid for one-year bank deposits after the rate cut.
"The market has digested the positive news," said Dai Yuzhong, a senior bond trader with China's J and A Securities Co. "In the next few months, it will not bubble so much again."
But analysts said Beijing's financial reforms this year, including changes in the way treasury bonds are issued, would continue to make the T-bill market active.
This year, the Finance Ministry has issued a great variety of short-term T-bills and long-term bonds, including three-month bills for the first time and a 10-year bond for the first time in a decade.
It has also added liquidity to the market by making the bulk of T-bills and bonds tradeable as from this year.

The central bank started trading state debts in open market operations in April, making commercial banks and other financial institutions more willing than ever to hold bills and bonds because of their increased liquidity, they said.
So far this year, China has issued a record 180 billion yuan of T-bills and bonds and market response has been good.
"Despite a record level of issues this year, both retail and institutional investors have snapped up T-bonds," said Lu of Guotai.
"This indicates their confidence in the bonds' returns, which will continue to support the T-bill market in future."
